name: Public Forum Debate
summary: Two teams of two debate a current-events question in speeches any thoughtful member of the public can follow.
who: High school (and middle school) students in teams of two. It was designed for citizen judges, so it is a friendly first event.
resolution: A current-events resolution that changes every month or two during the season.
sidesNote: A coin toss decides the order: the winner picks either a side (pro or con) or a speaking position (first or second), and the other team takes the remaining choice.

speeches.name: Crossfire (first speakers)
speeches.speaker: A1 & B1
speeches.job: Both first speakers ask and answer questions. The first question goes to the speaker who spoke first.

speeches.name: Second team, second speaker: Rebuttal
speeches.speaker: B2
speeches.job: Refute the other team's case and often answer the first rebuttal too.

speeches.name: Crossfire (second speakers)
speeches.speaker: A2 & B2
speeches.job: Both second speakers ask and answer questions.

speeches.name: First team, first speaker: Summary
speeches.speaker: A1
speeches.job: Narrow the round to the key issues and extend your best arguments.

speeches.name: Second team, first speaker: Summary
speeches.speaker: B1
speeches.job: Narrow the round to the key issues and extend your best arguments.

speeches.name: Grand Crossfire (all four debaters)
speeches.speaker: all
speeches.job: All four debaters question each other.

speeches.name: First team, second speaker: Final Focus
speeches.speaker: A2
speeches.job: Tell the judge, in plain words, why your team won.

speeches.name: Second team, second speaker: Final Focus
speeches.speaker: B2
speeches.job: Tell the judge, in plain words, why your team won.

prep.note: Three minutes for each team during the round (NSDA).

rewards: Clear explanations a citizen judge can follow
Good evidence on current events, explained, not just read
Weighing: telling the judge why your impacts matter more
start: Read the current topic and two or three background articles from different points of view.
Write a four-minute case for each side; you'll debate both.
Practice crossfire with a partner: short questions, short answers, no speeches.
Practice a two-minute final focus that a grandparent could follow.
varies: Prep time: NSDA uses three minutes per team; some leagues and tournaments use two or four.
Topic calendar: NSDA topics change every month or two; state leagues may use their own.
Some tournaments ban internet access during rounds; the NSDA allows it unless the tournament says otherwise.
Evidence rules (what a card must include, how fast you must produce it when asked) are set by each league.

p: Both teams present cases, then rebut each other, then narrow the round in summary and final focus. Three crossfires let debaters question each other directly. Because the judge may be a parent or a teacher with no debate experience, the best PF debaters explain each argument in everyday words and tell the judge exactly why it matters.
